newsitem.title: UK: Mark/lira at six-week highs as Europeans crumble.
newsitem.headline: Mark/lira at six-week highs as Europeans crumble.

text.p: The mark, despite falling to its lowest in nearly eight years against the dollar, continued to march higher against its European counterparts as they in turn succumbed to the U.S. currency's strength.
The mark rose most noticeably against the lira, rising to a six-week peak of 979.60 lire against its late Friday European level of 975.75/95. It had backed down to 978.65/90 by 1250 GMT.
The dollar's rise to 1,836.45 lire today, its highest against in more than a decade, was the main cause of mark/lira's gain, traders said.
There was also the effect of speculation the Bundesbank might change its policy regarding its key securities repurchase money market rate this week and allow market rates to rise.

Such expecations were sparked by the German central bank's decision on July 24, just before its four-week summer break, to fix the repo rate for the next two weeks at 3.00 percent and leave the options open for the remainder of its holiday.
"The market is taking on board the prospect of a possible German rate move, and the high-yielders are suffering, particularly Italy," said Mark Geddes, treasury economist at ABN AMRO here.
However, there was some scepticism about whether Germany was prepared to let interest rise purely for the sake of its currency, and whether such a move would help the mark substantially.

"If they switch to a floating repo rate or raise the fixed rate then it's likely a bit of mark buying would kick in. But if they don't do anything then the market's relief over that could lead to a lot of mark selling across the board," said Masahiro Kawasaki, manager at the Sakura Bank in London.
The mark gained most conspicuously against the lira because of the perception that Italy would suffer the most if the Bundesbank switched to a tightening policy.

That is because the Bank of Italy is in the midst of cutting rates to foster growth and would risk driving the economy further into recession if it reversed the process, analysts said. Italian gross domestic product shrank 0.4 percent in the first quarter from a year ago.

"The lira will be one of those that would suffer the most (from a German rate rise), while in other parts of Europe it wouldn't be too much of a blow. In France, they're waiting for the Bundesbank's next move so they can follow the Bundesbank's rate hike," said Sharda Persaud, economist at Banque Paribas.
The Italian bond market was also hit by German rate talk, undermining the lira. The yield spread between the key 10-year Italian BTPs and bunds widening to 103 basis points from 89 late on Friday.
However, despite such moves in the market, the Bundesbank was unlikely to let rates rise at this stage, as it would exacerbate the current weakness in the German economy, traders and analysts said.

"It would be premature to cut now, as we haven't seen evidence of strong inflationary pressures in Germany... It would mean that people would expect the euro to be slightly stronger than they have been thinking for the past few months, but the negative effects would outweigh the positive ones," Persaud said.
